posts.title: A Tuesday knee
posts.excerpt: When a patient presents with an acute joint injury, same-day MRI reporting enables general practitioners to establish definitive clinical management without weeks of uncertain waiting.
posts.content:
In general practice, managing an acute joint injury is frequently complicated by the delay between clinical assessment and diagnostic imaging. A patient twists a knee during a weekend run, attends their family doctor on a Tuesday morning with joint effusion and joint line tenderness, and faces the prospect of waiting days or weeks for an outpatient MRI slot and subsequent radiological report. During that interval, clinical uncertainty persists, work and exercise remain suspended, and patient anxiety mounts. At Nagi Imaging, our outpatient facility at 14 Calder Quay was established in 2016 specifically to resolve this disconnect for nearby medical practices.

A recent case referred by Dr. Nora Whelan of Ringsend Family Practice illustrates how our same-day reporting workflow operates in everyday clinical reality. At 10:15 on a Tuesday morning, Dr. Whelan evaluated a 42-year-old patient who had suffered an acute twisting injury to the right knee forty-eight hours prior. While mechanical locking was absent, marked medial joint line tenderness and a moderate joint effusion raised strong suspicion of an internal derangement involving the medial meniscus. Rather than issuing a standard referral slip into a delayed waiting system, Dr. Whelan contacted our referral line at +353 1 555 0148.

Our referrals coordinator, Grace Achterberg, reserved an appointment slot for 11:40 that same morning. The patient walked the short distance to our Grand Canal Dock imaging room, completed the routine pre-scan MRI safety screening, and was greeted by lead radiographer Tomás Oyelaran. Our high-field MRI scanner, installed in 2019, acquired high-resolution proton-density and T2-weighted multiplanar sequences over a calm, thirty-five-minute scan protocol. By 12:20, the patient had concluded the examination and was on their way home, with the complete digital imaging dataset transferred immediately onto our local archive.

Because every MRI performed at Nagi Imaging undergoes independent double reading, the study was reviewed by two consultant radiologists. Dr. Lukas Brenner, our musculoskeletal imaging specialist, completed the primary read within two hours of image acquisition, documenting an intact anterior cruciate ligament, mild joint effusion, and an undisplaced vertical tear within the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. Dr. Amira Haddad, our medical director, independently examined the cross-sectional series, verifying the stability of the tear margins and confirming the absence of chondral defects.

At 16:50—well before our standard 18:00 same-day cutoff for scans completed before 15:00—the finalized diagnostic report was digitally signed and transmitted directly into Ringsend Family Practice via our secure digital portal. When Dr. Whelan reviewed her afternoon clinical inbox, the report and high-resolution images were ready for review. She telephoned the patient that evening to outline the findings, prescribe targeted analgesia, and arrange structured conservative physical therapy, completely avoiding an unnecessary hospital emergency department visit.

This predictable timeline—referral in the morning, scan before midday, double reading in the afternoon, and an agreed treatment plan formulated before evening—embodies why Nagi Imaging was founded as a dedicated outpatient room. For general practitioners, prompt imaging changes patient management from reactive symptom surveillance to proactive, evidence-based care. When diagnostic questions are resolved on the same working day, patients avoid prolonged periods of workplace absence, unnecessary immobilisation, and repetitive consultations. By keeping our clinical focus anchored to nearby medical practices and our reporting turnaround strictly dependable, we ensure that diagnostic radiology operates as an immediate, responsive partner in primary patient care.

posts.title: Words a physio can use
posts.excerpt: Kofi Mensah, Harbourside Physiotherapy: a shoulder ultrasound described in plain terms.
posts.content:
When a shoulder rehabilitation stalled, Kofi Mensah sent his patient for an ultrasound at Nagi Imaging.

The report described the rotator cuff in plain words the exercise plan could follow, so the next session could start from what the scan showed.

posts.title: Last year’s images, side by side
posts.excerpt: Dr. Elena Popescu, Liffey Street Clinic: a chest CT follow-up with the comparison done.
posts.content:
A routine chest CT follow-up needs careful comparison. The radiologist set the new slices beside last year’s images and confirmed that nothing had changed.

The report reached Dr. Elena Popescu before the afternoon consultation, so the patient left with an answer the same day.
